posts.text: AI Agent and Agentic AI are not the same. The terms are often used interchangeably, but they describe two different levels of autonomy and system design. An AI agent is a goal-driven component. It reasons about a task, selects tools, maintains task state, observes results, and produces an outcome within a defined boundary. Agentic AI is the broader architecture. It coordinates multiple agents, workflows, systems, and decisions across longer-running processes. It can delegate work, share context, respond to events, recover from failures, and adapt using feedback. The difference becomes clearer across the stack: → AI agents use prompt context, session state, tool results, and conversation history. → Agentic systems require shared workflow state, cross-agent context, persistent memory, checkpoints, and recovery state. → AI agents commonly communicate through MCP, REST APIs, function calls, webhooks, SSE, and WebSockets. → Agentic systems add event buses, message queues, agent-to-agent communication, distributed workflows, and UI interaction. Reliability also becomes more complex. A single agent may need input validation, tool permissions, retries, timeouts, guardrails, and human approval. Agentic AI additionally requires policy engines, cross-agent permissions, approval gates, circuit breakers, least privilege, idempotency, audit trails, and failure recovery. The same applies to operations. Running one agent is an application problem. Coordinating many autonomous components is a distributed systems problem. An AI agent completes a task. Agentic AI coordinates an entire system to achieve a larger outcome.

posts.text: AI does not automatically reduce costs. It can lower operational expenses, automate repetitive work, speed up decisions, and help teams do more with fewer manual steps. But enterprise AI comes with a cost structure that is easy to underestimate. Every prompt consumes tokens. Every response uses inference capacity. Every agent workflow may trigger multiple model calls, tools, APIs, retrieval steps, and databases. Then add GPU infrastructure, vector storage, observability, security, evaluation, integration, and engineering time. Suddenly, “AI will save us money” becomes a much more complicated equation. The real question is not: “Can AI reduce costs?” It is: “Can this AI system create more business value than it costs to operate?” That means enterprises need to measure more than model accuracy. They need to track: → Cost per task → Tokens per workflow → Cost per successful outcome → Infrastructure utilization → Human hours saved → Automation rate → Error and retry costs → Revenue or productivity impact And this becomes even more important with AI agents. An agent might make 10, 20, or 50 calls to complete what looks like one simple request. Enterprise AI needs FinOps thinking from day one. Because the goal is not to build the smartest AI system. The goal is to build an AI system whose economics actually make sense at scale. ROI should be designed into the architecture, not calculated after deployment.

posts.text: Single-Agent vs Multi-Agent: Which One Do You Actually Need? Everyone wants to build a team of AI agents. Almost nobody checks if they need one. SINGLE-AGENT One agent runs the whole job — takes the goal, gathers context, plans, executes, checks its own work, delivers one answer. Use it when: the task has one clear objective, one agent can hold all the context, it's calling a few tools (not dozens), steps happen in order, and speed/cost matter more than depth. MULTI-AGENT A coordinator splits the goal among specialists (researcher, analyst, writer, critic, etc.) who work in parallel/sequence, then merges their output. Use it when: subtasks need genuinely different skills, work can run in parallel, a second opinion adds real value, and each stage needs its own check. The catch: every extra agent is another handoff — another place for context to drop, another cost, another thing to debug when it breaks. More agents ≠ more intelligence; it's more surface area for silent failure. Rule of thumb: Single-agent = one capable generalist. Multi-agent = a team, and a team needs a manager — that's you. Before your next architecture call, ask: "What breaks today if this stays one agent?" If no one has a specific answer, you don't need a team — you need a sharper single agent. posts.text: We may be creating more AI experts than AI results. I’m seeing an interesting phenomenon on LinkedIn. Every day there is another AI lifecycle. Another AI framework. Another “enterprise AI stack.” Another diagram showing agents, RAG, MCP, vector databases, orchestration, governance and 20 different tools. And apparently, knowing how to arrange those boxes now makes someone an AI strategist. Maybe I’m being overly critical—but after spending decades in IT, I think we’re missing something. Technology expertise isn’t the ability to describe technology. It’s the ability to make technology work in the real world. I’ve seen this movie before. We had ERP experts who knew every module but couldn’t get the business process right. Data experts who could build beautiful dashboards from questionable data. Cloud experts who moved workloads to the cloud without changing the economics. And now we’re seeing AI experts who can explain agents for 30 minutes—but may never have had to convince a CFO that the investment actually creates value. Enterprise AI isn’t primarily a model problem. It isn’t even primarily a tooling problem. It’s a business problem. Before asking “Which AI framework should we use?”, I’d rather ask: • What decision are we trying to improve? • What process are we trying to change? • Is our data good enough? • What happens when the AI is wrong? • Who is accountable? • What does this save or generate? • Can the organization actually adopt it? And perhaps the most important question: Would we still build this if we removed the word “AI” from the conversation? Because sometimes the answer is automation. Sometimes it’s better data. Sometimes it’s process redesign. Sometimes it’s traditional analytics. And sometimes, absolutely, it’s AI. That’s the distinction I see between AI literacy and AI leadership. You don’t need to know every new AI tool to lead an AI transformation. You need to understand the business, the technology, the data, the economics, the people and the risk—and know where AI genuinely belongs. The winners in enterprise AI won’t be those who can name the most frameworks. They’ll be those who can turn AI into measurable business outcomes. hashtag #EnterpriseAI hashtag #AILeadership hashtag #CIO hashtag #CTO hashtag #DigitalTransformation

posts.text: 🤖 Autonomous Multi-Agent Healthcare Orchestration on AWS How can payers and providers use Amazon Bedrock Agents, AgentCore, MCP, and secure tool-calling to coordinate healthcare workflows in parallel? Healthcare workflows often require eligibility checks, clinical validation, prior authorization, claims analysis, compliance review, and policy retrieval. Running everything sequentially is slow. Parallel delegation can reduce workflow latency and improve operational efficiency. 🏗️ The Architecture User Request → Orchestrator Agent → Delegated Agents → MCP Tools → Enterprise Systems → Results → Validation → Final Response The Orchestrator coordinates specialized agents: 🔹 Eligibility Agent → Coverage and benefits 🔹 Clinical Agent → Guidelines and medical necessity 🔹 Claims Agent → Authorization and claims rules 🔹 Compliance Agent → Privacy and policy checks 🔹 RAG Agent → Payer policies and clinical knowledge 🔹 Provider Agent → NPI and network validation ⚡ Parallel Execution Example Request: “Does this patient qualify for MRI prior authorization?” The Orchestrator delegates tasks: Eligibility Agent: Verify coverage Clinical Agent: Evaluate clinical criteria Claims Agent: Check authorization requirements RAG Agent: Retrieve current payer policies Compliance Agent: Validate access and handling requirements Each agent returns a structured result: Agent → Task → Evidence → Decision → Confidence → Risk → Next Action The Orchestrator aggregates the results and determines whether to recommend approval, request more information, or escalate to a qualified human reviewer. 🔐 Where AWS + MCP Fit Amazon Bedrock Agents: Model-driven task execution and tool use. AgentCore: Runtime, identity, memory, gateway, and multi-agent capabilities, where supported by the selected AgentCore services. MCP: A standardized interface for connecting agents to authorized tools and enterprise systems. GitHub + FHIR + SQL + APIs: Potential sources of versioned policies, clinical knowledge, and operational data. Every tool call should enforce identity, least privilege, PHI controls, authorization, auditability, and result validation. ⚠️ Important: Parallel execution does not automatically make decisions faster or safer. Use deterministic orchestration, bounded delegation, and human approval for high-impact clinical and financial actions. 💼 Why It Matters One orchestrator. Multiple specialized agents. Coordinated execution. The result: ⚡ Faster administrative workflows 🔐 Stronger security boundaries 📋 Better auditability 📈 Scalable payer and provider operations 🤝 More efficient human decision-making The future of healthcare AI is not just smarter models. It's secure, observable, multi-agent orchestration that turns enterprise data into coordinated action. hashtag #AgenticAI hashtag #AIAgents hashtag #AWS hashtag #AmazonBedrock hashtag #BedrockAgents hashtag #AgentCore hashtag #MCP hashtag #HealthcareAI hashtag #FHIR hashtag #RAG hashtag #AISecurity hashtag #AIArchitecture hashtag #LLMOps hashtag #CloudSecurity #HealthcareAI#EnterpriseAI hashtag #AIGovernance hashtag #MultiAgent

As agents multiply, so do the opportunities for context loss, conflicting outputs, and silent propagation of error. This is where runtime governance becomes essential: continuously verifying the operational reality and determining whether the next action should be ALLOWED, MODIFIED, DEFERRED, ESCALATED, or REFUSED. Absolutely — I think “architectural trust boundaries” is exactly the right framing. A handoff should not automatically inherit the authority or admissibility of the previous agent. Each boundary should trigger a new runtime check: Is the context still valid? Is this agent authorized for the next action? Are the assumptions and evidence still sufficient? And is the proposed action still admissible under the current human and operational reality? In that sense, multi-agent governance may need to treat every consequential handoff as a new decision boundary, not merely a communication event. The chain of accountability must travel with the task — but the right to act should be re-earned at each

posts.text: Everyone wants to build a team of AI agents. Almost nobody has checked if they need one. This breakdown lays out single-agent vs multi-agent architecture below. Here's what it shows, then the question that decides which one is worth building. SINGLE-AGENT One agent runs the whole job start to finish. It takes the goal, gathers context, plans the steps, pulls the data, calls the tools it needs, checks its own work against guardrails, and hands back one answer. Use it when: → The task has one clear objective → One agent can hold all the context it needs → It's calling a handful of tools, not dozens → The steps happen in order, not in debate → Speed and low cost matter more than depth MULTI-AGENT A coordinator splits the goal into pieces and hands them to specialists, a researcher, an analyst, a writer, a critic, a visualizer, who work in parallel or in sequence, track progress on a shared board, and get checked against guardrails before anything moves forward. The coordinator merges it all into one output. Use it when: → The subtasks need genuinely different skills → Pieces of the work can run at the same time → A second opinion would catch something the first missed → Parallel work saves real time, not just looks better in a demo → Each stage needs its own check before moving on Here's the part the diagram can't show you, and the part that matters most if you're the one signing off on this. Every additional agent is another handoff. Another place where context can quietly get dropped between steps. Another component someone on your team has to watch, and pay for, whether it's earning its keep or not. None of that shows up in the demo. All of it shows up in the first incident review. I've watched a team add a critic agent to a workflow that had one task and nothing to disagree about. It didn't improve the output. It added a step, a cost, and one more thing to debug when something broke. This is the core of what I call the Enterprise Agent Stack: infrastructure and coordination have to earn their place before you add them, not the other way around. More agents is not more intelligence. It's more surface area for something to go wrong quietly. A rule that holds up in practice: single-agent is one capable generalist. Multi-agent is a team, and a team needs a manager. Someone on your side has to be that manager. Before your next architecture conversation, skip "what could a specialist agent do here" and ask this instead: What breaks today if this stays one agent? If nobody in the room has a specific answer, you don't need a team yet. You need a sharper single agent. 💾 Save this for your next architecture decision. ♻️ Repost to help someone in your network avoid this mistake. 🔔 Follow Gabriel Millien for daily insights on closing the AI Execution Gap. 𝐌𝐚𝐥𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐦𝐞𝐝 𝐓𝐨𝐨𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐬: Free-text generation isn't constrained to your API schema, so agents invent arguments that don't exist. They call functions that were deprecated last week. 𝟒. 𝐑𝐮𝐧𝐚𝐰𝐚𝐲 𝐋𝐨𝐨𝐩𝐬: No hard stop on retries means infinite loops, and one misconfigured workflow can burn $3,000 in API calls. You find out when the invoice arrives, not when it happens. 𝟓. 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐭 𝐈𝐧𝐣𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧: Untrusted input can hijack the agent's behavior, so a customer email changes what it does. A webpage redirects it to execute something else. 𝟔. 𝐒𝐡𝐢𝐩𝐩𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐨𝐧 𝐕𝐢𝐛𝐞𝐬: Demos are one happy-path run you retried until it looked good, but production is thousands of unattended runs with a non-deterministic model. Real systems charge cards and write rows. 𝟕. 𝐍𝐨 𝐎𝐛𝐬𝐞𝐫𝐯𝐚𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐲: You can see the request and response, but everything in between is opaque. When it breaks, you have no traces and no way to debug. posts.text: AI agents need more than intelligence. Giving a team access to powerful models may create impressive demos, but enterprise value begins when those agents can perform real work safely, reliably, and repeatedly. The journey starts with clear business goals. Choose measurable use cases, define success metrics, secure executive sponsorship, and identify workflows where autonomy can create visible outcomes. Then build the foundation: → Governed data and trusted knowledge → Permission-aware retrieval → Clear agent goals and constraints → Approved tools, APIs, and actions → Human escalation and rollback paths A reliable enterprise agent follows a continuous loop. It gathers context, retrieves trusted knowledge, reasons about the request, creates a plan, uses tools, validates the result, and escalates when human judgment is required. Production introduces another level of responsibility. Teams need observability, access control, auditability, safety checks, incident handling, latency monitoring, cost tracking, and continuous evaluation. Without these controls, scaling autonomy also scales operational risk. The maturity path usually looks like this: Assistants → Task Agents → Workflow Agents → Controlled Autonomy → Production Operations → Coordinated Systems Each stage increases capability, but also demands stronger governance and coordination. The real goal is not to deploy the maximum number of agents. It is to build a governed system where agents, tools, data, and humans work together to deliver reliable business outcomes. Enterprise agentic AI is not one model. It is an operating model.

posts.text: AI governance has a timing problem. Not always a policy problem. Most enterprise controls were built for human-paced work. Access reviews happen quarterly. Policies are approved annually. Models are validated periodically. Committees review incidents later. That rhythm worked when change happened in batches. Agentic AI works differently. An agent can plan, execute, call tools, retry actions, and react to new data continuously. The model may stay the same. But the operating context can change every minute. That creates the real gap: AI can act faster than the organization can control. So governance needs more than a review calendar. It needs three layers: ✅ Machine-speed controls Limits, policy checks, anomaly detection, and automatic suspension. ✅ Event-driven human review Immediate attention when risk patterns change. ✅ Periodic governance Leaders review patterns, update thresholds, and improve the control system. The real question is not: “Do we have AI governance?” It is: Can our controls move at the speed of AI risk?

posts.text: AI Product Engineering is where capability becomes a product — and where weak decisions become expensive. That is the thinking behind: AI ELEMENTS™ | 05 The Periodic Table of AI Product Engineering The table maps 60 elements across 10 disciplines, but the real value is not in knowing the terms. It is in using them to make better product decisions. For example: Problem & Decision Design → What decision are we improving, and where should AI stop? Data, Context & Knowledge → What information must the product trust before it can act? Model & Capability Design → Which model capability is sufficient for the job? Interaction & Experience Design → What should the user see, control, approve, or override? Agent & Workflow Engineering → Which actions can be automated, and where must a human remain in the loop? Evaluation & Reliability → What evidence is required before this behavior is considered production-ready? Governance & Safety → What happens when the model is wrong, uncertain, or misused? Deployment & Operations → How will we monitor, recover, and update the product over time? Economics & Value Realization → What does one successful business outcome actually cost? Adoption, Change & Scale → Will people trust it enough to use it repeatedly? That is the larger point: AI Product Engineering is the discipline of turning probabilistic capability into reliable product behavior. A model demo can prove that something is possible. A product has to prove that it is useful, dependable, governable, affordable, and worth adopting. That is a very different standard. posts.text: 9 takeaways on how CFOs should think about AI ROI (from Baker Tilly's Technology Finance Symposium): 1. Not every workflow needs an agent. If you can describe every step and the data is structured, traditional automation is likely cheaper at the same quality. 2. Agents make sense when the use case requires flexibility, like "resolve this customer issue." The signs are: 1) unstructured data, 2) rapidly changing processes, 3) a predefined recipe doesn't work well. Agents handle ambiguity better, but they need governance because they don't follow a fully defined set of steps. 3. Fix the process before you automate it. Teams often point technology at a broken process and end up "moving the cheese just to move the cheese." If you can't say what should happen, stop and define that first. Business process redesign is an understated part of implementing AI. 4. Measure the right metrics. It's easy to say AI "handles x% of Level 1 support requests." It's harder to say what that does to customer satisfaction and retention over time. The metrics that matter often lag and are harder to quantify. 5. Frame the investment "to move [metric] from [X] to [Y] over [Z period]." The best metrics go beyond productivity and tie to economic outcomes. For example: Increased outbound SDR activity should lead to more sales calls, more opportunities, higher win rates, and increased new ARR. 6. Most companies underestimate the total cost. It goes beyond tokens and subscriptions. Data storage and management can account for over half of the investment. Human review and rework also add cost (a Sage study shows this "verification tax" can eat up a quarter of the expected efficiency in some cases). 7. Most companies struggle with forecasting. A study suggests that only 11% of companies can forecast AI spend with ±10% accuracy, largely because they lack visibility into costs by agent or use case. 8. Use the right model for the right job. Purpose-built, context-specific models improve output quality while controlling cost (my translation: don't always just default to Fable or Opus). 9. Apply software development rigor. Finance teams can build on their own now, but few of us have been taught how to ship what we build. Sound engineering discipline needs robust testing and validation; otherwise, things will break in production. Learning the software development lifecycle will be a new useful skill. Thank you, Chris Price Stuart Langer Ray Rike, for an insightful panel. What jumped out at you?

posts.text: I built a LinkedIn outreach engine last week, then forbade it from sending anything for seven days. 30 messages written and scored. Zero delivered. Shadow mode is there because these resources don't refund. 15 InMail credits a month. An invite to a specific person is a card you play once. I assumed the risk was message quality. Every draft already clears a rubric before it gets logged, so that part was covered. The shadow log said the problem was somewhere else. I'd split the month across three lanes: 84 invites for hiring managers, 50 for customers, 34 for people I want in my orbit. Seven days of queue produced 28 job, 1 customer, 1 authority. 93 people viewed my profile in that window. The targeting only knew how to see one kind of them. Run live, I'd have spent real invites 28-to-1 against a plan I wrote myself, and the scorecard would have read as working, because the lane that was firing is the one with the shortest feedback loop. Shadow mode costs a week of talking to nobody. I booked 4 calls in that window anyway, all from the inbox, none from outreach. Still open: I can't tell a lane that's genuinely empty from a lane my search queries can't see.

posts.text: When I left IBM, I knew I didn’t want to spend the next chapter of my career simply talking about AI—or even just designing and building algorithms for large corporations. I wanted to build something that could actually move the needle. For more than 30 years, I’ve built and deployed AI solutions for large organizations. I also served four years on IBM’s AI Ethics Board and became a leading voice on responsible AI, algorithmic bias, and the harm these systems can create. I didn’t come to this issue only through research. I completed my PhD in Artificial Intelligence with research focused on algorithmic bias and real-world harm. I also wrote Hidden in White Sight, examining how bias can become embedded in the technologies and systems shaping people’s lives. But my perspective has never been purely academic. It has been shaped by decades of actually building and deploying the kinds of systems we are now being asked to govern. That led me to an uncomfortable reality: The value organizations see in building and deploying AI will almost always outweigh the perceived risk of the bias or harm that AI might produce. No matter what we believe, advocate for, or warn against, AI adoption is not slowing down. As one technology CEO has said, the horse is already out of the barn. Organizations are not going to stop building AI. Nor should they. The real question is whether we will build the accountability and safeguards necessary to understand what these systems are doing—and address the harm when they get it wrong. That is why I founded Xtegrity. I brought together a small team of senior technology leaders with experience at IBM, Google, and Microsoft to help turn that vision into a platform designed to change how organizations understand and manage AI risk. Xtegrity moves AI governance beyond policies, checklists, frameworks, and conversations—and toward action. It enables organizations to simulate potential harm before AI causes it, identify and deter harmful outcomes, quantify the financial risk of AI harm, and govern models where they already operate—across clouds and environments—without moving models or sensitive data. Perhaps most importantly to me, Xtegrity creates a pathway for people who believe they have been harmed by AI to identify that harm and connect directly with the organizations responsible for the models. I’ve done a lot of talking. I’ve done a lot of research. I’ve built a lot of technology. But at some point, talking about responsible AI is not enough. We have to build something that makes responsibility real. That is what Xtegrity represents for me. As we build increasingly powerful AI systems, we must also build the mechanisms to understand their risk, anticipate their harm, quantify the consequences—and hold them accountable. Today, I’m introducing Xtegrity to the world. Over the next few weeks, we’ll share more about the platform and our official launch event. This is what we’ve built
